newsitem.title: USA: U.S. envoy welcomes Chinese courting of Congress.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy welcomes Chinese courting of Congress.

text.p: The U.S. ambassador to Beijing on Wednesday welcomed as long overdue China's reported effort to match Taiwan's influence on the U.S. Congress.
"In times past, they've been their own worst enemy as far as Congress is concerned," said James Sasser, sworn in as ambassador in January 1996 after three terms as a U.S. senator from Tennessee.
Sasser, citing his own personal views, described stepped-up Chinese lobbying as a desirable counterweight to Taiwan's well-documented ability to woo members of Congress.
"I think it's a healthy sign for them to try to get their case, put their case forward with Congress," he told a breakfast hosted by the local arm of the Asia Society, a private educational group.
Sasser did not discuss allegations that Chinese officials may have crossed the line from legal lobbying into possibly illegal efforts to buy influence over U.S. foreign policy.

The Justice Department is investigating reported evidence that Chinese embassy officials in Washington sought to secretly steer foreign donations toward President Bill Clinton's 1996 re-election campaign, officials familiar with the probe have said. The embassy has denied any such effort.

In an interview after his speech, Sasser said Chinese officials had not spoken to him about the status of the Justice Department probe. He said the matter was having no effect that he was aware of on any aspect of bilateral ties.

Sasser tied China's thinking about the need to woo Congress to lobbyists' role in the 1995 decision to let Taiwanese President Lee Teng-hui attend his 50th college reunion at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York.
"I think that when Lee Teng-hui was granted a visa to the United States, the Chinese suddenly realized that the Congress could be just as important as the Executive Branch," he said.

The visit was the first by a Taiwanese leader to the United States since 1979, when Washington established full diplomatic ties with Beijing and downgraded links with Taiwan, regarded by China as a renegade province.

It plunged Chinese-U.S. relations into a steep tailspin from which they have only recently emerged, contributing to Beijing's decision to stage menacing war games off Taiwan in March 1996. The United States responded by sending two aircraft carrier battle groups to the region.
A Chinese diplomat confirmed that the embassy had boosted the size of its congressional liaison office "over time", but declined to cite numbers or to peg it to Lee's visit.
The congressional liasion office is headed by Shao Wenguang, an Oxford-educated career foreign service officer with the rank of minister counselor, the diplomat said.
Sasser said he had personally advised Chinese officials to invite members of Congress to visit China, adding that 20 percent of the 535 members of the House and Senate had made the trip in January.

Sasser said he expected Vice President Al Gore to visit China in the last week of this month and that the United States hoped to welcome President Jiang Zemin this November. Clinton planned to return the state visit to Beijing sometime next year, he said.
